AIRPORT FOLLOWINGS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A spate of airport followings hit the city of Jo’burg – we investigate the modus operandi behind this growing crime trend.

Unique Selling Point:
GROWING CRIME TREND - INTERNATIONAL IMPACT ON SOUTH AFRICA's IMAGE

CCTV VIDEO FOOTAGE OF ROBBERIES

INSIDER HIDDEN IDENTITY INTERVIEW


Summary:
Criminals target tourists, businessmen and even locals using spotters to identify prime targets – they follow the mark, and move in when the opportunity arises making off with thousands of rands in stolen goods, foreign exchange and jewelry.

We cast the spotlight a crime trend that seems to gaining momentum again.

THERE IS A LOT OF CONTENT AND INSIGHT INTO THIS CRIME TREND - DEFINITELY 10 MIN WORTH :)

Further information:
WHO DO THEY CRIMINALS TARGET?
Mostly foreign businessmen and tourists – these are people that are in the country for a short while and will usually not be able to testify if there are any arrests made as they would have already left the country. They are also targeted because they usually have foreign currency or cash South African money on them. Businessmen usually carry laptops and electronics.

HOW DO THEY SELECT THE VICTIMS?
The theory is that there are spotters in the airport who sit and identify targets. Recently a lot of African foreigners coming in on from African countries – the wealthy travellers are easy to spot – the type of luggage and the way they dress. They also target Chinese Nationals, along with Indian businessmen who come in on African flights.
Travelers arriving from big shopping destinations like Dubai – it’s almost guaranteed that the targets will have valuable goods in their luggage.
But the selection appears to be random – there aren’t any patterns – it’s not that all the victims were stopped by customs, or that they all took taxi’s or that they all went to foreign exchange – it’s completely random.

WHAT IS THE MO WHEN THE HIT THE TARGET?
There are three MO’s which supports the theory that there is more than one syndicate operating.

MO 1
Three plain clothed men, pull over the car showing a paper / badge to give the impression that they are cops – usually using an unmarked car. They don’t take the car – only luggage and valuables. Often foreigners don’t know what our police uniforms look like and they don’t realise that plain clothed men in unmarked cars are suspicious….

MO 2
The victims are followed to their homes and knocked in the drive ways or as in our one case study’s experience at the entrance of a shopping centre.

MO 3
People are knocked as they leave hotels or as they arrive back from exchanging money or having gone to buy jewelry – this supports the theory that hotel staff or drivers could be involved.

WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING?
There is increased security in and around the airport with big roadblocks slowing down and dispersing traffic. There is a task team working on it. But they have very few leads – often these hits happen where there isn’t CCTV footage available – the cases that have footage are rare.

CASE STUDIES
JEREMY PETERS – SHARONLEA RESIDENT – JANUARY 2017
There is CCTV footage. Incident took all of four minutes. Four armed men pulled up behind them in their driveway and made off with suitcases and valuables.
He picked up his family form OR Tambo on a Sunday morning in January. “Since my family had huge luggage, I went straight to the pickup park, loaded their luggage and proceeded”.
He said he didn’t notice that he was being followed as it was raining.
As soon as he opened the gate when he got home, he saw a man approaching. “From the way he approached us, I just knew it was a robbery. [Because of the trailer], I couldn’t reverse out of the yard [quickly].”
“When he [tapped on the window] with the gun, I opened the door and did not want to compromise the safety of my family,” he said.
The man, who was wearing a hoodie, asked him if he had a gun and told him he would shoot him if he disobeyed him. While his accomplice ransacked the trailer and the vehicle’s boot, the man took their wallets, cellphones, rings and jackets.

BASIE VORSTER – EDENVALE RESIDENT / AFRICAN BUSINESSMAN – MARCH 2017
Basie also has CCTV footage – he arrived at OR Tambo on a flgiht from the DRC. His wife picked him up at the arrivals parking area. They drove off and went to a shopping centre to have dinner. They were knocked at the entrance of the centre. The criminals made off with at least R100k worth of good and gear.

KEN COPELAND – DRIVER – APRIL 2017
Ken was driving a group of 10+ tourists from the airport – he was pulled over at the Rivonia off ramp by three men in civilian clothes with an unmarked vehicle giving the impression that they were cops. They took cellphones, foreign currency and local money.

INTERVIEWS
LODEWYK MURRAY – PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR
Lodewyk has worked on a number of these cases for foreign nationals and has a clear understanding of the modus operandi, and how criminals have adapted their methods as investigators close in on them. He speaks to the challenges of getting prosecutions, because the victims often have left the country.

INFORMANT – HIDDEN IDENTITY
We get inside info from a man that works closely with one of these syndicates – he will explain how they select targets, how much they pay spotters and how they get rid of the valuables.

SAPS
I’ve asked for an interview with Minister Mbalula – if he can’t or won’t – then we will have someone from the HAWKS. I’ve asked to be allowed to film at the roadblocks outside OR TAMBO.

PRIVATE SECURITY COMPANIES
This year has seen an increase of robberies where victims have been targeted – this has lead to a demand for VIP Armed Escorts – we interview a security company that uses bullet proof Mercs and other vehicles to transport executives from big multi-nationals. This speaks to impact these robberies are having on South Africa’s international image from an investor perspective.

TOURISM BUSINESS COUNCIL OF SOUTH AFRICA
They have kept their own statistics relating to robberies at hotels and followings from airports and have an international safety and security team that have put together guidelines and interact with the tourism industry to improve safety and SA’s image around this crime trend that appears to largely target foreigners.

Press Release:


Airport Heist
Criminals are following tourists, businessmen and even locals from the OR Tambo airport, robbing them at gunpoint of cash, electronics and valuables. But these heists can
only be successfully pulled off with the help of airport insiders. So who is behind this spate of violent robberies in Johannesburg? Carte Blanche investigates a crime trend
that’s gaining momentum.

Script:


TRANSCRIPTS AIRPORT FOLLOWINGS

VO: OR Tambo International Airport is the gateway to South Africa, welcoming visitors from all corners of the world.

But – it is also, where an old crime trend is rearing its ugly head again, targeting tourists, business people and even locals in a spate of airport following robberies.

VISH: The situation for us has reached unprecedented levels – so much so, that it’s giving us sleepless nights.
TSHIFHIWA: We are starting to see more and more people on a weekly basis being followed home and these incidents are starting to be more and more vicious.

VO: Since the beginning of the year there have been 19 confirmed incidents linked to OR TAMBO, four of them this last week alone saw three people shot and wounded.

A trend that could seriously cripple the tourism industry. Tshifhiwa Tshivhengwa is from the Federated Hospitality Association of South Africa.

TSHIFHIWA: This is becoming more frequent and it’s becoming more concerning and it’s denting the image of South Africa as far as tourist starting to look at us and say wait a minute – am I really safe coming into South Africa.

LINK: To the trained eye targets aren’t simply passengers but may unwittingly advertise themselves – from the clothes they wear to their jewellery, to their luggage set and of course their point of origin – all these are key indicators that can turn you into a mark.

BASIE: I was disgusted, I wasn’t half an hour in my own country and I got robbed. //

VO: In March, Basie Vorster had just arrived from a two month work trip in the Democratic Republic of Congo. His wife picked him up at OR Tambo International airport and headed home.

BASIE: I said to her what are we eating tonight, she said instead of going home, lets go have some sushi. // And as we stopped at the shopping centre, // we got out of the car and that’s when they hit the car.

VO: Basie is convinced they were followed from the airport.

BASIE: They knew exactly which car they were looking for. // It was a case of coming in straight away, stop right next to vehicle, broke the window, and pull it out.
BONGANI: What did they take?
BASIE: I had two laptop bags and two big suitcases with me. // within two minutes they were done.

VO: They took goods worth a R100 000.

LODEWYK: – it’s not opportunistic – it’s organised.

VO: Private Investigator Lodewyk Murray – says Basie’s hit was a textbook operation.

The criminals mostly target early morning and early evenings flights, often from other African countries - these passengers usually carry cash and electronics.

The robbers trail the mark, then they move in when the opportunity arises, they pull weapons on the victims, and make off with thousands of rands in luggage, foreign exchange and jewellery, in a matter of minutes.

LODEWYK: // It’s a whole operation // they spot clients getting off international flights // it is all inside information, as soon as they arrive from the plane, go through the gates, they have people observing them.

VO: This man is a spotter – he is employed in the airport. Let’s call him Steven, he gives the robbers information on possible targets – for a fee.

INSIDER: We are placed in different franchises or enterprises // It can be anything from car rentals to securities to porters to cleaners – people that work within // they get details, registrations, check what you’re carrying,// your movements //

VO: A second group that deliver big bounties, are people coming from shopping destinations usually with brand new items in their luggage.

INSIDER: it’s things that are just getting easier with people on the inside, people on the outside.
BONGANI: Are we ever going to put an end to this or is it just too lucrative?
INSIDER: it’s easy money – // why do you need to work for a month if you can make it in a day.
BONGANI: How much do spotters get paid?
INSIDER: Anything from R200 to R3000 / R4000 Depending on the value of what they are working on – the value of the robbery.

VO: Jeremy Peters picked up his parents and brother who’d arrived from the United States via Dubai.

JEREMY: I was at the pick up because I had trailer with me and there was a lot of luggage that my parents were coming with // I managed to pick them up, load the luggage in the trailer and the boot and left the airport.

VO: But unbeknownst to Jeremy – they’d been spotted and were being followed.

This is CCTV footage from Jeremy’s home. As he pulls into the driveway, the car is approached by a man.

JEREMY: // the minute he pulled out the gun, I was ok – I know what’s happening and I opened the door and complied. // I thought they wanted the vehicle – no, they wanted the luggage.

VO: Here you see the robbers pulling in their vehicle. While two men were taking cellphones, jewellery and money from Jeremy and his family – three others went straight to the trailer and started loading the luggage.

JEREMY: They took had a lot of electronics they had brought from the States for us here in South Africa, iPads, iPhones, iWatches, the also had a lot of clothes that they brought back and also they did a lot of shopping in Dubai - so the value of the goods that were taken was around R300k.

VO: Jeremy is certain there were airport employees involved – the robbers took everything, except, for two bags.

JEREMY: one of two things it could be that they couldn’t fit in their vehicle or that they knew which bags to take –The bags that they left behind didn’t have any valuable belongings in them.

VO: A theory Basie supports, having personally worked for the company that did the airport scanner installations years ago.

BASIE: I know how that operates within – the x-ray machine – your luggage goes through that and then what happens is they can see what is valuable in those suitcases.

VO: Airport spotter Steven says while some insiders are disgruntled employees motivated by quick cash – some of them have no choice but to pass out information.

INSIDER: // Guys get threatened into doing it as well, criminals know where you live, they know you’re a guard at a certain place or you’re a porter at a certain place – they threaten your family and force you to do something.

LINK: Although South AFricans are also victims of this type of crime – the majority of targets are foreigners – both business people and tourists because they are simply unprepared for the threat.

VO: Private Security specialist, Waal de Waal provides security for international corporate clients – he believes the spotters are trained.

WAAL: Lets face it, these guys do profiling, // if you give them a flight and you tell me who is the South African and who not – I promise you they will be spot on – if you walk through that door – they’ll say foreigner local, foreigner, foreigner, local and you know they do their homework, // their reconnaissance – and that’s scary.

TSHIFHIWA: it’s worrying that we have to tell tourists // this is how you have to be dressed when you come to South Africa // put your camera in the bag –you cannot be free – what is the point of a vacation is you can’t be free?

VO: According to Tshifiwa, we need to get a handle on these robberies, because it could have dire consequences for the tourism industry.

TSHIFHIWA: The issue of safety is coming back to the table – and it is one of those issues we have worked hard to eradicated as an industry // – but the issue of crime and the perception of the destination not being safe, it does have an impact.

LINK: This is not an exaggerated fear – the threat is real – multinational companies are even resorting to using close protection services and will go to any lengths to protect their executive clients.

WAAL: The extreme level is where we put a chopper in the air // a birds eye view from the top just to protect and prevent.

VO: Waal says the demand for close protection services with armoured vehicles and specialist drivers from his company increased by 29% in the last two months.

WAAL: it looks normal, but if you just look at the windows, you can see how thick it is – this vehicle is armoured right through // All the doors plated, the engine, the back, the boot, the roof, everything.
BONGANI: That kind of sounds extreme
WAAL: it sounds extreme because we’re dealing with a real threat currently.

VO: One of the tactics that foreigners fall victims to, is fake roadblocks.

LODEWYK: It will happen in about a 5 km radius around the airport //the suspects will pull them off with a reflective jacket, ask them to pull off and that is when the robbery will commence.

VO: While one robber deals with the passengers, another will get the luggage from the boot.

BONGANI: it does seem that they are becoming more violent now?
LODEWYK: Yes, //they want to come in and take the targets items and be out within 5 / 6 minutes - they don’t have time to struggle or ask you nicely for your items

VO: Sunday a week ago, two citizens from the Democratic Republic of Congo were followed after taking an UBER from the airport to their hotel in Sandton. They were robbed, shot and wounded.

LODEWYK: They produce their firearms, they want you just to hand it over – if you do not, you suffer the consequences – they are extremely violent.

TSHIFHIWA: it is something that needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency. //Tourism has a huge impact on the economy – it is one of the industries that is growing and it is one of the industries that could even take us out of this junk status

VO: But with no arrests in the majority of cases, it looks like these robbers are above the law.

JEREMY: I guess in South Africa, we become accustomed to these things and we accept the status quo // I believe that the country should protect me in going to work and back and paying my taxes. And at this point in time, I don’t see that as being the case.

VO: Lodewyk is personally aware of 8 cases this year where not a single arrest has been made.

LODEWYK: The foreigners isn’t going to stay here to open up criminal cases – so most of these crimes go unattended or uninvestigated

VO: The South African Police Services’ Brigadier Vish Naidoo says these cases are still a priority, and prosecutable.

VISH: As long as we have a statement and we have sufficient evidence to support that statement – we can resort to prosecution on a state case – it’s difficult to do that – but it can be done.
BONGANI: Why not make arrest faster?
VISH: it always helps to arrest the suspect faster – for us in any case the first 24 hours is critical – because the longer it takes to identify and arrest the perpetrator the more difficult it becomes in any crime,

VO: But the time for excuses is running out – action is needed says Tshifhiwa.

TSHIFHIWA: // What has been done now hasn’t been working – so we need to figure out what the next level of intervention that is need from the policing point of view.

LINK: So why can’t the police catch these guys – well it’s not that simple – this is a highly organised intricate web of criminals from using cloned plates on rental cars to carefully choosing hijacking spots to make sure there can be no footage – once these guys make off with your goods – they disappear.

BONGANI: These syndicates, are we talking local guys? Who are they?
INSIDER: //You get your chancers and then you get your professionals - It changes – different people, different races, it changes all the time.

VO: But Brigadier Naidoo says the police are going to be closing in on these syndicates as they cast the net wide.

VISH: We working through intelligence networks, not only in South Africa but also with our counterparts from abroad.
BONGANI: Is there a task team?
VISH: // the police management has decided we have to enhance the police capacity that is involved in the policing of airports proactively as well as reactively – we have taken steps now to enhance the visible policing environment which means to enhance patrols on identified routes – to enhance crime intelligence capacity – detective capacity to make sure that we investigate cases successfully to ensure successful prosecutions.

VO: Tshifhiwa hopes the police will deliver results sooner than later.

TSHIFHIWA: // we cannot afford to let criminals win over this thriving industry. // this is not a battle that we can afford to loose.



* ASKED ACSA FOR INTERVIEW TELEPHONICALLY & IN WRITING – THEY DECLINED IN WRITING.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 30 June 2017 Press Release: Airport Heist Criminals are following tourists, businessmen and even locals from the OR Tambo airport, robbing them at gunpoint of cash, electronics and valuables. But these heists can only be successfully pulled off with the help of airport insiders. So who is behind this spate of violent robberies in Johannesburg? Carte Blanche investigates a crime trend that’s gaining momentum. Script: TRANSCRIPTS AIRPORT FOLLOWINGS VO: OR Tambo International Airport is the gateway to South Africa, welcoming visitors from all corners of the world. But – it is also, where an old crime trend is rearing its ugly head again, targeting tourists, business people and even locals in a spate of airport following robberies. VISH: The situation for us has reached unprecedented levels – so much so, that it’s giving us sleepless nights. TSHIFHIWA: We are starting to see more and more people on a weekly basis being followed home and these incidents are starting to be more and more vicious. VO: Since the beginning of the year there have been 19 confirmed incidents linked to OR TAMBO, four of them this last week alone saw three people shot and wounded. A trend that could seriously cripple the tourism industry. Tshifhiwa Tshivhengwa is from the Federated Hospitality Association of South Africa. TSHIFHIWA: This is becoming more frequent and it’s becoming more concerning and it’s denting the image of South Africa as far as tourist starting to look at us and say wait a minute – am I really safe coming into South Africa. LINK: To the trained eye targets aren’t simply passengers but may unwittingly advertise themselves – from the clothes they wear to their jewellery, to their luggage set and of course their point of origin – all these are key indicators that can turn you into a mark. BASIE: I was disgusted, I wasn’t half an hour in my own country and I got robbed. // VO: In March, Basie Vorster had just arrived from a two month work trip in the Democratic Republic of Congo. His wife picked him up at OR Tambo International airport and headed home. BASIE: I said to her what are we eating tonight, she said instead of going home, lets go have some sushi. // And as we stopped at the shopping centre, // we got out of the car and that’s when they hit the car. VO: Basie is convinced they were followed from the airport. BASIE: They knew exactly which car they were looking for. // It was a case of coming in straight away, stop right next to vehicle, broke the window, and pull it out. BONGANI: What did they take? BASIE: I had two laptop bags and two big suitcases with me. // within two minutes they were done. VO: They took goods worth a R100 000. LODEWYK: – it’s not opportunistic – it’s organised. VO: Private Investigator Lodewyk Murray – says Basie’s hit was a textbook operation. The criminals mostly target early morning and early evenings flights, often from other African countries - these passengers usually carry cash and electronics. The robbers trail the mark, then they move in when the opportunity arises, they pull weapons on the victims, and make off with thousands of rands in luggage, foreign exchange and jewellery, in a matter of minutes. LODEWYK: // It’s a whole operation // they spot clients getting off international flights // it is all inside information, as soon as they arrive from the plane, go through the gates, they have people observing them. VO: This man is a spotter – he is employed in the airport. Let’s call him Steven, he gives the robbers information on possible targets – for a fee. INSIDER: We are placed in different franchises or enterprises // It can be anything from car rentals to securities to porters to cleaners – people that work within // they get details, registrations, check what you’re carrying,// your movements // VO: A second group that deliver big bounties, are people coming from shopping destinations usually with brand new items in their luggage. INSIDER: it’s things that are just getting easier with people on the inside, people on the outside. BONGANI: Are we ever going to put an end to this or is it just too lucrative? INSIDER: it’s easy money – // why do you need to work for a month if you can make it in a day. BONGANI: How much do spotters get paid? INSIDER: Anything from R200 to R3000 / R4000 Depending on the value of what they are working on – the value of the robbery. VO: Jeremy Peters picked up his parents and brother who’d arrived from the United States via Dubai. JEREMY: I was at the pick up because I had trailer with me and there was a lot of luggage that my parents were coming with // I managed to pick them up, load the luggage in the trailer and the boot and left the airport. VO: But unbeknownst to Jeremy – they’d been spotted and were being followed. This is CCTV footage from Jeremy’s home. As he pulls into the driveway, the car is approached by a man. JEREMY: // the minute he pulled out the gun, I was ok – I know what’s happening and I opened the door and complied. // I thought they wanted the vehicle – no, they wanted the luggage. VO: Here you see the robbers pulling in their vehicle. While two men were taking cellphones, jewellery and money from Jeremy and his family – three others went straight to the trailer and started loading the luggage. JEREMY: They took had a lot of electronics they had brought from the States for us here in South Africa, iPads, iPhones, iWatches, the also had a lot of clothes that they brought back and also they did a lot of shopping in Dubai - so the value of the goods that were taken was around R300k. VO: Jeremy is certain there were airport employees involved – the robbers took everything, except, for two bags. JEREMY: one of two things it could be that they couldn’t fit in their vehicle or that they knew which bags to take –The bags that they left behind didn’t have any valuable belongings in them. VO: A theory Basie supports, having personally worked for the company that did the airport scanner installations years ago. BASIE: I know how that operates within – the x-ray machine – your luggage goes through that and then what happens is they can see what is valuable in those suitcases. VO: Airport spotter Steven says while some insiders are disgruntled employees motivated by quick cash – some of them have no choice but to pass out information. INSIDER: // Guys get threatened into doing it as well, criminals know where you live, they know you’re a guard at a certain place or you’re a porter at a certain place – they threaten your family and force you to do something. LINK: Although South AFricans are also victims of this type of crime – the majority of targets are foreigners – both business people and tourists because they are simply unprepared for the threat. VO: Private Security specialist, Waal de Waal provides security for international corporate clients – he believes the spotters are trained. WAAL: Lets face it, these guys do profiling, // if you give them a flight and you tell me who is the South African and who not – I promise you they will be spot on – if you walk through that door – they’ll say foreigner local, foreigner, foreigner, local and you know they do their homework, // their reconnaissance – and that’s scary. TSHIFHIWA: it’s worrying that we have to tell tourists // this is how you have to be dressed when you come to South Africa // put your camera in the bag –you cannot be free – what is the point of a vacation is you can’t be free? VO: According to Tshifiwa, we need to get a handle on these robberies, because it could have dire consequences for the tourism industry. TSHIFHIWA: The issue of safety is coming back to the table – and it is one of those issues we have worked hard to eradicated as an industry // – but the issue of crime and the perception of the destination not being safe, it does have an impact. LINK: This is not an exaggerated fear – the threat is real – multinational companies are even resorting to using close protection services and will go to any lengths to protect their executive clients. WAAL: The extreme level is where we put a chopper in the air // a birds eye view from the top just to protect and prevent. VO: Waal says the demand for close protection services with armoured vehicles and specialist drivers from his company increased by 29% in the last two months. WAAL: it looks normal, but if you just look at the windows, you can see how thick it is – this vehicle is armoured right through // All the doors plated, the engine, the back, the boot, the roof, everything. BONGANI: That kind of sounds extreme WAAL: it sounds extreme because we’re dealing with a real threat currently. VO: One of the tactics that foreigners fall victims to, is fake roadblocks. LODEWYK: It will happen in about a 5 km radius around the airport //the suspects will pull them off with a reflective jacket, ask them to pull off and that is when the robbery will commence. VO: While one robber deals with the passengers, another will get the luggage from the boot. BONGANI: it does seem that they are becoming more violent now? LODEWYK: Yes, //they want to come in and take the targets items and be out within 5 / 6 minutes - they don’t have time to struggle or ask you nicely for your items VO: Sunday a week ago, two citizens from the Democratic Republic of Congo were followed after taking an UBER from the airport to their hotel in Sandton. They were robbed, shot and wounded. LODEWYK: They produce their firearms, they want you just to hand it over – if you do not, you suffer the consequences – they are extremely violent. TSHIFHIWA: it is something that needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency. //Tourism has a huge impact on the economy – it is one of the industries that is growing and it is one of the industries that could even take us out of this junk status VO: But with no arrests in the majority of cases, it looks like these robbers are above the law. JEREMY: I guess in South Africa, we become accustomed to these things and we accept the status quo // I believe that the country should protect me in going to work and back and paying my taxes. And at this point in time, I don’t see that as being the case. VO: Lodewyk is personally aware of 8 cases this year where not a single arrest has been made. LODEWYK: The foreigners isn’t going to stay here to open up criminal cases – so most of these crimes go unattended or uninvestigated VO: The South African Police Services’ Brigadier Vish Naidoo says these cases are still a priority, and prosecutable. VISH: As long as we have a statement and we have sufficient evidence to support that statement – we can resort to prosecution on a state case – it’s difficult to do that – but it can be done. BONGANI: Why not make arrest faster? VISH: it always helps to arrest the suspect faster – for us in any case the first 24 hours is critical – because the longer it takes to identify and arrest the perpetrator the more difficult it becomes in any crime, VO: But the time for excuses is running out – action is needed says Tshifhiwa. TSHIFHIWA: // What has been done now hasn’t been working – so we need to figure out what the next level of intervention that is need from the policing point of view. LINK: So why can’t the police catch these guys – well it’s not that simple – this is a highly organised intricate web of criminals from using cloned plates on rental cars to carefully choosing hijacking spots to make sure there can be no footage – once these guys make off with your goods – they disappear. BONGANI: These syndicates, are we talking local guys? Who are they? INSIDER: //You get your chancers and then you get your professionals - It changes – different people, different races, it changes all the time. VO: But Brigadier Naidoo says the police are going to be closing in on these syndicates as they cast the net wide. VISH: We working through intelligence networks, not only in South Africa but also with our counterparts from abroad. BONGANI: Is there a task team? VISH: // the police management has decided we have to enhance the police capacity that is involved in the policing of airports proactively as well as reactively – we have taken steps now to enhance the visible policing environment which means to enhance patrols on identified routes – to enhance crime intelligence capacity – detective capacity to make sure that we investigate cases successfully to ensure successful prosecutions. VO: Tshifhiwa hopes the police will deliver results sooner than later. TSHIFHIWA: // we cannot afford to let criminals win over this thriving industry. // this is not a battle that we can afford to loose. * ASKED ACSA FOR INTERVIEW TELEPHONICALLY & IN WRITING – THEY DECLINED IN WRITING. VISH: The situation for us has reached unprecedented levels – so much so, that it’s giving us sleepless nights. metadata.Summary: Criminals target tourists, businessmen and even locals using spotters to identify prime targets – they follow the mark, and move in when the opportunity arises making off with thousands of rands in stolen goods, foreign exchange and jewelry. We cast the spotlight a crime trend that seems to gaining momentum again. THERE IS A LOT OF CONTENT AND INSIGHT INTO THIS CRIME TREND - DEFINITELY 10 MIN WORTH :)
metadata.Further information: WHO DO THEY CRIMINALS TARGET? Mostly foreign businessmen and tourists – these are people that are in the country for a short while and will usually not be able to testify if there are any arrests made as they would have already left the country. They are also targeted because they usually have foreign currency or cash South African money on them. Businessmen usually carry laptops and electronics. HOW DO THEY SELECT THE VICTIMS? The theory is that there are spotters in the airport who sit and identify targets. Recently a lot of African foreigners coming in on from African countries – the wealthy travellers are easy to spot – the type of luggage and the way they dress. They also target Chinese Nationals, along with Indian businessmen who come in on African flights. Travelers arriving from big shopping destinations like Dubai – it’s almost guaranteed that the targets will have valuable goods in their luggage. But the selection appears to be random – there aren’t any patterns – it’s not that all the victims were stopped by customs, or that they all took taxi’s or that they all went to foreign exchange – it’s completely random. WHAT IS THE MO WHEN THE HIT THE TARGET? There are three MO’s which supports the theory that there is more than one syndicate operating. MO 1 Three plain clothed men, pull over the car showing a paper / badge to give the impression that they are cops – usually using an unmarked car. They don’t take the car – only luggage and valuables. Often foreigners don’t know what our police uniforms look like and they don’t realise that plain clothed men in unmarked cars are suspicious…. MO 2 The victims are followed to their homes and knocked in the drive ways or as in our one case study’s experience at the entrance of a shopping centre. MO 3 People are knocked as they leave hotels or as they arrive back from exchanging money or having gone to buy jewelry – this supports the theory that hotel staff or drivers could be involved. WHAT ARE THE COPS DOING? There is increased security in and around the airport with big roadblocks slowing down and dispersing traffic. There is a task team working on it. But they have very few leads – often these hits happen where there isn’t CCTV footage available – the cases that have footage are rare. CASE STUDIES JEREMY PETERS – SHARONLEA RESIDENT – JANUARY 2017 There is CCTV footage. Incident took all of four minutes. Four armed men pulled up behind them in their driveway and made off with suitcases and valuables. He picked up his family form OR Tambo on a Sunday morning in January. “Since my family had huge luggage, I went straight to the pickup park, loaded their luggage and proceeded”. He said he didn’t notice that he was being followed as it was raining. As soon as he opened the gate when he got home, he saw a man approaching. “From the way he approached us, I just knew it was a robbery. [Because of the trailer], I couldn’t reverse out of the yard [quickly].” “When he [tapped on the window] with the gun, I opened the door and did not want to compromise the safety of my family,” he said. The man, who was wearing a hoodie, asked him if he had a gun and told him he would shoot him if he disobeyed him. While his accomplice ransacked the trailer and the vehicle’s boot, the man took their wallets, cellphones, rings and jackets. BASIE VORSTER – EDENVALE RESIDENT / AFRICAN BUSINESSMAN – MARCH 2017 Basie also has CCTV footage – he arrived at OR Tambo on a flgiht from the DRC. His wife picked him up at the arrivals parking area. They drove off and went to a shopping centre to have dinner. They were knocked at the entrance of the centre. The criminals made off with at least R100k worth of good and gear. KEN COPELAND – DRIVER – APRIL 2017 Ken was driving a group of 10+ tourists from the airport – he was pulled over at the Rivonia off ramp by three men in civilian clothes with an unmarked vehicle giving the impression that they were cops. They took cellphones, foreign currency and local money. INTERVIEWS LODEWYK MURRAY – PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR Lodewyk has worked on a number of these cases for foreign nationals and has a clear understanding of the modus operandi, and how criminals have adapted their methods as investigators close in on them. He speaks to the challenges of getting prosecutions, because the victims often have left the country. INFORMANT – HIDDEN IDENTITY We get inside info from a man that works closely with one of these syndicates – he will explain how they select targets, how much they pay spotters and how they get rid of the valuables. SAPS I’ve asked for an interview with Minister Mbalula – if he can’t or won’t – then we will have someone from the HAWKS. I’ve asked to be allowed to film at the roadblocks outside OR TAMBO. PRIVATE SECURITY COMPANIES This year has seen an increase of robberies where victims have been targeted – this has lead to a demand for VIP Armed Escorts – we interview a security company that uses bullet proof Mercs and other vehicles to transport executives from big multi-nationals. This speaks to impact these robberies are having on South Africa’s international image from an investor perspective. TOURISM BUSINESS COUNCIL OF SOUTH AFRICA They have kept their own statistics relating to robberies at hotels and followings from airports and have an international safety and security team that have put together guidelines and interact with the tourism industry to improve safety and SA’s image around this crime trend that appears to largely target foreigners.
